document.title: Ambassador Dean Cable, "Subject: Indian Handling of Afghanistan"
document.authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
document.note: Action cable describing Indian leaders' confusion over the U.S. reaction to Indian efforts on an Afghan settlement. Gandhi perceives that Washington resents increased Indian activism; Kaul was given a démarche about a meeting with Zahir Shah in Rome. Dean suggests a reassuring Reagan letter.

events.description: Gorbachev announces in Moscow a new initiative on Afghanistan with early, front-loaded Soviet withdrawal.
Indian Ambassador Kaul meets U.S. State Department officials; warned against Indian conduct of contacts.
Natwar Singh meets former King Zahir Shah in Rome.
Per press reports, Cordovez meets the Afghan resistance leadership.
Ronen Sen has a brief talk with the Pakistani ambassador in New Delhi about Indian contacts on Afghanistan.
Dean sends cable recommending a presidential reply to Rajiv Gandhi's letter.
Gandhi met the US President in Washington and was urged to be more active on Afghanistan.
Ambassador Kaul met US State Department officials; warned against Indian conduct of contacts.
Ronen Sen briefly talked with the Pakistan Ambassador in New Delhi about Indian contacts.
Natwar Singh met former King Zahir Shah in Rome.
Cordovez reportedly met the Afghan resistance leadership.
Gorbachev announced a new Afghanistan initiative in Moscow including early, front-loaded Soviet withdrawal, with advance notice to Gandhi.
Dean met Ronen Sen, who delivered Gandhi's letter to the US President (second conversation Feb 9).
Dean cabled State recommending a swift presidential reply to Gandhi and encouraging India-Pakistan communication.

sources_cited: Rajiv Gandhi's personal letter to the President
key_claims: Rajiv Gandhi believes the U.S. resents India's increased activism on Afghanistan.
Dean argues India is already a player in Afghanistan diplomacy, if a minor one.
The Soviets appeared to support India's role, shown by early notice of Gorbachev's announcement to Gandhi.
Gandhi thinks his involvement helped Gorbachev decide on early, front-loaded Soviet withdrawal.
Dean recommends a swift presidential letter to Gandhi and urges continued India-Pakistan communication on Afghanistan.
The Rome meeting of Natwar Singh and Zahir Shah was not prevented by the U.S. demarche.
